note_tweet.text:
The best AI coding agent isn’t necessarily the one that wins a benchmark.

It’s the one that helps you ship real software—with less friction, better context, and your judgment still in control.

That’s why I’m choosing Grok Bot with Cursor for my current QuantLab workflow.

I build and sell Python futures trading bots through HFTCODE. My work isn’t just generating a function from a prompt. It’s maintaining strategy code, reviewing risk checks, updating dashboards, documenting changes, and running the business around those products.

The market doesn’t wait for me to finish copying code out of a chat window.

Here’s what drives my decision. 🧵👇

First: the edit loop matters more than the chat demo.

A model can produce a beautiful snippet and still be a poor fit for daily development.

Can it work across the actual project?
Can it recognize helpers that already exist?
Can it propose changes across multiple files?
Can I inspect the diff, run checks, and reject a bad assumption without leaving the editor?
That’s the appeal of Grok Bot with Cursor for me: keeping AI assistance close to the code, rather than making me the manual bridge between a chatbot and my repository.
Second: repository discipline is an AI productivity tool.
A messy repo creates expensive confusion—for humans AND agents.

Duplicate modules. Unclear entry points. Research dumps mixed with production code. Undocumented interfaces.

All of that leads to repeated explanations, wasted context, and patches aimed at the wrong problem.

For my mix of Python tooling and denser C++ components, clean structure is non-negotiable:

→ Separate experiments from production strategy logic.
→ Keep interfaces documented.
→ Make changes reviewable through branches and pull requests.
→ Store important project knowledge somewhere more durable than a chat history.

I’m not claiming a magic percentage reduction in token costs. I’m saying that avoiding repeated work saves time and money.

Third: my business doesn’t stop at the repository.

HFTCODE runs on Shopify. There’s also email automation, content, distribution, and payments to manage.
An assistant that helps with code but leaves every business task as a copy-paste exercise solves only part of my problem.
The platform integrations described in my article are a major reason Grok Bot appeals to me.
The workflow I want is practical: prepare a Shopify article as a hidden draft, help shape content for the email system I use, and keep those tasks close to the development work.

Prepare—not publish without permission.

Fourth: I’m evaluating the whole stack, not declaring every other model bad.

Meta Muse has produced useful code in my experience. But without the tight major-IDE connection I need, it isn’t my daily driver.

Cline with VS Code has helped me get work done. I’m moving away because my confidence in that setup’s direction has weakened—not because VS Code suddenly stopped being a serious editor.

That’s my assessment, not an audited market-share finding.

Copilot with GitHub has an obvious integration advantage, but for my workload, the output hasn’t consistently justified the price relative to alternatives.

And I’m still watching Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini as their coding environments and integrations evolve.

“For now” is an important part of this decision.

Fifth—and most important—faster coding cannot mean weaker review.

Trading software is an unforgiving place to confuse confidence with correctness.

An agent can introduce a bad fill assumption, overlook a session calendar, or “simplify” a risk check in ways that quietly change the system’s behavior.

My rule stays the same regardless of which model I use:

Agents propose. I review and approve.

Anything involving live trading, broker credentials, paid campaigns, public publishing, or other money-sensitive actions stays behind an explicit human approval gate.

A useful assistant should make that review easier—not encourage me to skip it.

If you’re choosing your own AI coding stack, don’t just ask it to generate a clever demo.

Give it a real multi-file task in your repository.

Measure how much context you have to paste.
Check whether it respects existing architecture.
Inspect the quality of the diff.
Count the corrections it needs.
Compare the total time to a reviewed, usable result.

Then test the business workflows around the code.

That’s a much better buying decision than choosing on brand recognition or subscription price alone.

For QuantLab, the combination I’m prioritizing is:

IDE-native work + clean repositories + useful platform integrations + accountable human review.

Right now, that points to Grok Bot with Cursor.

Good tooling won’t rescue a broken trading strategy. But it can make sound engineering easier to inspect, maintain, and ship.

An iMessage style app for you & your AI agents that live across the leading platforms. The app where you can coordinate your Muse agent with your Grok Bot in the same group chat.

AgentMsgr runs no AI itself. Your agents do the thinking, on the subscriptions you already pay for. We just built the messaging layer on top, and its free to use today.

How to set up: [VIDEO]

1. Tap Add agent
2. Pick where your agent lives (Grok Bot, Meta Muse, or Other for anything with an email inbox)
3. Tap Get the pairing message and copy it
4. Paste it into your agent's own app and hit send
5. Your agent connects itself. You never type an email address.

Repeat for each agent. One pasted message each.

Then make the group:

6. Tap New chat, pick your agents, name the group
7. Every agent sees every message. No @mention means anyone can answer, and the rest only jump in with something new
8. Want one agent? Tap its chip or @mention it

→ The planner split the work
→ Grok Bot pulled the top customer complaint
→ The writer used it in headlines without being asked
→ OpenClaw started building the page
→ Grok drafted the launch posts and sent an approval card before posting anything

Assign your agents an email, coordinate them in an iMessage style user interface.

Free to start. Link in the reply.

What Dulus does.

What the Dulus desktop app does — never how it does it. Everything on this page ships in the app you download from https://t.co/DwzYbOlPo2, built from Interant. Things that exist only in our internal tooling aren't listed.

At a glance: 114 built-in tools · 123 commands · 40+ model provider integrations · up to 26 agents at one table · ~1,800 MCP servers in the market · 14 themes · 34 languages.

The Round Table:
• Up to 26 seats, any mix of models. Put different models at one table, on the same problem, at the same time.
• A shared task board. Seats claim, update and finish tasks you can see and edit.
• A table that organizes itself. Leaders plan and assign, so seats stop stepping on each other's work.
• Call a seat by name. A seat that already finished its turn comes back in the same round when another seat calls on it.
• Decisions to make. What only you can decide arrives as a card: the question, the context, numbered options with their consequences, a recommended pick and what it's holding up. Answer one by one from the keyboard; the seat that asked hears your answer live. Works from the terminal and Telegram too.
• The live view. A drawing of the table built only from real events — words flowing from each seat, messages crossing the table, tasks traveling to their owners, decisions rising to you. Take a photo, record an MP4, or hide the text before you share it.
• The Tasks board. Group by status or by seat, drag a card to reassign it, chain dependencies, see what's waiting on you, and jump back to the same live table.
• Smooth at scale. Tested with 25 agents and 60,000 history entries on one page.

Hands on your computer:
• See, click and type in any app — in any language, accents, ñ and emoji included — on Windows, macOS and Linux.
• Reads the screen in light and dark mode, and finds the word you asked for even with accents or small misreads.
• A live overlay while it drives. Follow the conversation over full-screen apps without it ever stealing your keyboard.
• Approve or stop from the overlay. Permission prompts appear on top of whatever app is open; the stop button ends the turn.
• A real browser. A Chromium pane inside the app where you watch the agent browse.
• A live terminal panel. Watch the actual shell the agent is using, command by command.
• Long jobs in the background. Hand off long tasks and keep chatting; the job wakes Dulus up when it's done.
• A persistent Python console. Working memory that lives outside the context window.

Voice:
• Astral Voice. A hands-free conversation: it listens, thinks and starts talking before the reply is finished.
• Cut in anytime. Interrupt it mid-sentence and it stops to listen.
• A real transcript. Full messages beside the orb, with formatting, timestamps and the line being spoken highlighted.
• Dictation in the chat box. Talk into the composer; your words stay a draft until you send them.

Your phone:
• Telegram bridge. The same conversation from your phone: text, voice notes, photos, albums and files.
• Live progress with a stop button, approvals and questions as buttons, and generated images delivered as photos.
• Pair with a link or a QR code. It keeps answering even while the desktop window is hidden.
• WebChat. The same chat in any browser, including your phone on your local network.

Memory:
• Profiles and projects. Memories stay with the profile and project they came from, so separate profiles never mix.
• Facts with a lifecycle. A newer memory on the same subject replaces the old one, facts that go stale get flagged for re-checking, and old memories are archived — never silently deleted.
• Crash-proof. A crash in the middle of a write can't corrupt your memories; damage is detected and repaired on boot.
• Loopback. The whole conversation stays searchable after it's compacted. Ask "where were we?" and get a real answer.
• Search everywhere. Reach the memories of every other workspace when you ask for it.

Models:
• 40+ provider integrations, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini and Vertex, AWS Bedrock, Azure, DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, GLM, MiniMax, Meta, Perplexity, Cloudflare Workers AI and Runware.
• Local models with Ollama and LM Studio.
• Dulus's own hosted models, paid by the token in Fuel. No keys needed.
• One reasoning dial. A single 0–4 thinking setting that works the same on every model.
• Big windows. Up to a million tokens where the provider offers it, and a context meter that counts everything actually sent.
• Cache-friendly by design. Requests stay stable across tools and turns, so providers can cache them and long sessions cost less.
• Learned models. Any model you use for more than ten replies joins the autocomplete on its own.
• Batch jobs at batch prices where the provider offers them.
• Resilient. A silent retry when a provider is overloaded, and an honest error — never an empty reply — when a stream drops.

Create:
• Astral Images. Generate with FLUX.2, GPT Image, Gemini and Imagen, Meta Muse or Runware models — or type any provider/model id. Add references, and drag any result back in as a reference to keep iterating.
• Video with Veo, Sora 2 and Runware video models.
• Images from any chat. Any chat model that can use tools can generate an image mid-conversation.
• Knows what your keys unlock. From the first message, Dulus knows which image, video and voice capabilities your keys enable — it only checks which keys exist, never their values.
• Artifacts. A library for the documents and mini apps the agent builds: versions, previews, source and downloads. Mini apps run isolated, and your images, videos and reports show up there too.
• Reports. Rich HTML reports that open in their own window and stay linked in the chat history.

Extend:
• MCP market. About 1,800 servers with complete setup recipes, runtimes included, with servers and secrets kept per profile and secrets encrypted at rest.
• AutoAdapter. Point it at a GitHub repo and get tools — each one verified before it's switched on.
• Plugins you can toggle and reload live, per profile.
• Skills — bundled ones, plus skill directories you can search and install from.
• Tool packs. Switch optional packs on and off — Mr. Dulus, Solana, live data feeds and a codebase graph — and see what each one costs in tokens before you do.
• Live data with sources. Markets, crypto and economic indicators, each value with its unit, date and source.
• Sub-agents. Delegate work to background agents — up to three at once, nested three deep, optionally each in its own git worktree.

Control:
• Permission modes: auto, manual, accept-all and plan.
• Approvals everywhere — in the app, the pet, the overlay and Telegram. The first answer wins.
• Steer mid-task. A bubble over the chat box lets you message Dulus while it works; it reads your note before its next step. Whatever you were typing when it finished moves into the chat box.
• A Stop that really stops. A hung command is killed the moment you press Stop, and your next message goes straight through.
• Checkpoints, undo and fork. Rewind a conversation or branch it, and back sessions up to a private GitHub Gist.
• Audit trail and budgets. See what the agent wrote, edited, ran and clicked, and set limits on what it can spend.
• Proactive check-ins and reminders. Dulus can come back to you on its own.

The desktop app:
• A native app for Windows, with macOS and Linux builds published on the download page as they're ready.
• Dulus OS — a web desktop with its own apps, inside the app.
• A desktop pet — a small companion with its own chat, approvals and a stop button.
• A nudge when the reply is ready. If you switched away, the taskbar (Windows), the Dock (macOS) or the window (Linux) lets you know. No notifications.
• Keyboard-first. Start typing anywhere and it goes to the chat box.
• Tidy tool calls. Consecutive tool calls fold into one row you can open.
• Fuel wallet. Balance, a deposit address with a QR code, and your history.
• Automatic updates on Windows.
• 14 themes and 34 languages.
• Closing the window closes everything. No orphan processes left behind.

🤖 An AI assistant for a mom with three kids might be a better startup idea than building another ChatGPT.

👉 Silicon Valley is going all in on personal AI assistants.

And the money pouring into this space is getting ridiculous.

👉 According to TechCrunch and Dealroom:
• 24 personal AI assistant startups covered by TechCrunch
• 49 startups tracked by Dealroom
• $1.8B invested in 2026 alone

One of the biggest names right now is Instinct (https://t.co/yHztidKFiu).

🚀 And it's not your typical AI app.
You don't need to install anything.

📲 The assistant runs on its own cloud computer, talks to you through iMessage or WhatsApp, and can keep working even when you're not around.

Need a flight booked? Just text it.

Groceries? Same thing.

It can even call a restaurant to make a reservation or contact your bank about some random charge you don't recognize.

Basically, you tell it what you need, and it handles the boring stuff.

💰 Now look at the valuation.
In August, Instinct was valued at $2.5B.

Just 33 days later?

$10B.

And according to founder Noah Shinn, they spent $0 on marketing.

😅 Meanwhile, the big players are jumping in.

Meta launched Muse, which reportedly hit 2.8 million downloads in just 12 days.

OpenAI introduced Dots in late September.

So yeah, this market is getting crowded pretty quickly.

🧠 But here's what caught my attention.

Not all personal AI assistants are trying to solve the same problems.

💡You can roughly split them into four groups.

1. General-purpose AI assistants
• Instinct: https://t.co/yHztidKFiu
• Poke: https://t.co/TudVzBlc0e
• Martin: https://t.co/nM8u0qFqym
• Tomo: https://t.co/YsE3Y57Fue
• Tab: https://t.co/Xw9rh34NKx

The idea is to handle almost anything you ask.

Book trips, shop, schedule, make calls, and manage everyday tasks.
Basically, one assistant for your entire life.

2. AI assistants for work
• Town: https://t.co/wqJftsx9RB
• Catch: https://t.co/cmwjvmpr9g

These focus on emails, calendars, meetings, and all the administrative work that eats up your day.

💸 Town reportedly raised $108M at a $1B valuation.

Pretty serious money for an AI assistant that helps people get through their inboxes and schedules.

3. AI assistants for specific groups of people

This category might actually be the most interesting.

👨‍👩‍👧 For parents and families:
• Ollie: https://t.co/LbSHrs1l9Y
• Ohai: https://t.co/fTDgibP8om
• Fambot: https://t.co/Z7QHnafWOr
• Orbits: https://t.co/skYUArRDSe

Think about a mom with three kids.

School emails, soccer practice, doctor's appointments, birthday parties, permission slips, family calendars.

Now imagine having an assistant that sorts through all those messages, picks out what matters, and keeps the family's schedule organized.

That's a real problem for a very specific group of people.

🎬 For content creators:

There's Stanley: https://t.co/jjzZNaeUan

It helps turn voice notes into posts, suggests content ideas, publishes content, and tracks performance.
Same general AI technology, but built for a completely different audience.

4. AI assistants backed by real humans
Because sometimes AI just can't finish the job.

Poke has a feature called Poke Human.

If something requires a real person, like making a difficult reservation or handling a phone call, a human can step in.

Miso (https://t.co/xqOQEV96we) takes a similar approach to travel.

AI helps plan the trip, while people handle the messy parts like airline miles, complicated connections, and cancellations.

💡 And there's one interesting detail about Instinct.

According to its founder, more than half of all transactions on the platform are travel-related.

👉 Think about that.

A company valued at $10B is building an assistant that can supposedly do almost anything.

But over 50% of its transaction activity comes from travel ✈️

One category.

🚨 That's where I think the real opportunity might be for smaller founders.

Trying to compete with OpenAI, Meta, or a $10B startup on a general-purpose assistant?

Good luck with that 🥴
But building an AI assistant specifically for a mom with three kids?

Something that handles school emails, kids' schedules, appointments, reminders, and all the little things parents deal with every day?

That's a much more focused problem.

And you don't need to build an AI that can do everything.

You just need to build one that does a few things really well for a specific audience.

Big tech is trying to build an AI assistant for everyone.

❓Maybe the better opportunity for a solo founder is building one for someone very specific.
